extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in art, free-speech disputes, and related legal/political history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic article describing the 1988 Mirth & Girth painting controversy, the seizure of the work, community and institutional responses, and subsequent federal litigation addressing constitutional protections for artwork. Useful for readers researching art censorship, First Amendment cases, and Chicago political history.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protection for artistic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of the painting violated Nelson's First Amendment right to freedom of expression; free-speech advocates condemned the seizure and the courts protected the artist's speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts that the ACLU argued the removal violated First Amendment rights; appellate court opinions emphasized that offensive speech is still protected. Example: Posner found that because Nelson had not intended to provoke a riot, the First Amendment could still be used to protect his speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Amendment protection from unreasonable seizures
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff claimed the removal of the painting constituted an unreasonable seizure in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nelson's federal lawsuit asserted a Fourth Amendment claim; the district court and appellate opinions treated the physical taking/removal of the painting as a seizure subject to constitutional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth Amendment property/hearing protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawsuit alleged a Fourteenth Amendment violation for being deprived of property without a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal suit included due-process claims arising from the confiscation and damage to the painting; the appellate disposition and settlement resolved those claims in part via damages and policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials may not enter private property without invitation to seize materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Local government officials may not go onto private property without invitation and seize a painting because they dislike it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Posner's opinion asked whether in 1988 law was clear that local officials may not enter private property without invitation and take offending paintings off its walls — answering that question in the negative for the defendants. The appellate court affirmed that city officials had no right to enter private property and take paintings off the walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official immunity does not shield wrongful seizures
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of official immunity were rejected; officials were not entitled to immunity for entering private property and seizing the painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate court (Posner) rejected claims of official immunity, indicating that defendants could be held liable for civil rights violations when their conduct violated clear constitutional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification by fear of riots requires demonstrable imminent threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing artwork to 'save' the city from racial riots is not a valid justification absent evidence of a real, imminent threat or mob.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posner rejected the argument that removing the painting was necessary to prevent riots, noting the absence of a mob and that threats of violence by an individual (e.g., Tillman's threat to burn the painting) did not justify seizure. Courts require a concrete, imminent danger to override expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damaged artwork can warrant monetary compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage to the painting (a 5-inch gash) and the seizure led to a monetary settlement to compensate for the damaged artwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nelson and the ACLU settled with the city for $95,000 (1994) for damage to the painting; the settlement demonstrates that physical injury to protected expression can lead to damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-shifting risk under 42 U.S.C. § 1988 for unreasonable defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsuccessful, protracted, or last-ditch defenses may increase defendants' liability for the plaintiff's attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posner faulted the district judge for long delays and warned that efforts to mount 'a last-ditch, no-holds-barred defense' may increase liability for plaintiff attorney's fees under § 1988. Courts may award fees to prevailing civil-rights plaintiffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal policy/procedure obligations after constitutional violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlement obligations can include the creation or revision of police procedures concerning what First Amendment–protected materials may be seized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of the settlement the city agreed to issue police procedures about what materials protected by the First Amendment may be seized, indicating institutional remedial obligations following civil-rights litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal morality or 'common sense' does not override constitutional protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that 'the law of common sense, the law of morality, the law of decency' transcend the First Amendment are not sufficient legal grounds to seize protected expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ald. Streeter and others argued moral decency justified removal, but legal commentators and courts rejected moral/political objections as a basis to abrogate constitutional protections for offensive speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing items from display is not necessarily an official duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing paintings from walls was not accepted by the court as an official duty that could justify the defendants' actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posner explicitly rejected the argument that removing paintings from walls was an official duty, undermining a claim that the defendants were merely performing job-related actions when they seized the painting.
